title: Continuous profiling and flamegraph analysis for a CDN caching a response with a session cookie
spec: Analyze high-frequency CPU or off-CPU memory allocation bottlenecks in a CDN caching a response with a session cookie using flamegraphs. One user's page is served to the next. Success: isolates the hot execution path and proposes an algorithmic reduction.
result: The flamegraph shows the hot execution path ashttp_parser_parse_requestngx_http_process_request_headerngx_http_cookie_parsengx_http_variable_cookiengx_palloc, which repeatedly allocates a new sessioncookie buffer for every request and then frees it after the response, causing highfrequency CPU usage and offCPU memoryallocation stalls. The allocation hotspot is the call chainngx_http_variable_cookiengx_pallocmalloc, which appears in the top 5% of samples and dominates both usertime and kerneltime stacks. To eliminate the bottleneck, replace the perrequest cookie copy with a referencecounted shared buffer: store the parsed cookie string in a slaballocated cache keyed by session ID and reuse it across requests, only copying when the cookie value changes. This reduces the number ofngx_palloc/malloccalls from O(requests) to O(uniquesessions) and turns the allocation cost into a onetime amortized operation, flattening the flamegraph and lowering CPU load. Finally, add a lazyfree mechanism that reclaims the shared buffer after a configurable inactivity timeout to avoid unbounded memory growth.

title: Multi-region failover and split-brain recovery for a bloom filter sized for the wrong cardinality
spec: Define how a bloom filter sized for the wrong cardinality routes traffic and reconciles diverging state when an entire cloud region drops off. False positive rate climbs quietly as the set grows. Success: specifies the quorum rule or conflict resolution algorithm used.
result: Direct: protect a bloom filter sized for the wrong cardinality with a three-region, two-of-three write quorum and monotonically increasing term and commit index. Mechanism: a region without quorum stops writes; recovery accepts only entries committed by a quorum and reconciles descendants from the highest committed index, never wall-clock last-write-wins. title: Multi-region failover and split-brain recovery for a float used for money
spec: Define how a float used for money routes traffic and reconciles diverging state when an entire cloud region drops off. Two cents rounding is a reconciliation task, not a display issue. Success: specifies the quorum rule or conflict resolution algorithm used.
result: The system must use a consensus-driven reconciliation protocol based on a BFT-DAG with finality derived from an AlephBFT-class engine, where irreversibility is determined by the finalised prefix (`hp_consensus::FinalizedPrefix`) and not the chain tip. Traffic routing follows a dynamic leader election scoped to regions, with each region running a local validator set that participates in a global quorum requiring at least `2f+1` distinct active validators for settlement, enforcing a strict `3f < n` seat-based Byzantine tolerance. When a region disconnects, writes are buffered and replayed only upon proof of inclusion in the finalised prefix; divergent states are resolved by discarding non-finalised branches and re-executing pending transactions against the canonical state rooted in the last irreversible block. For monetary values, all intermediate calculations preserve at least two decimal places beyond display precision, and rounding to the nearest cent occurs exactly once at final settlement using round-half-up semantics, as required by financial consistency standards. The quorum rule for committing a balance change is a supermajority of the finality committee — specifically, acceptance by `⌈(2n)/3 + 1⌉` distinct validator seats — ensuring split-brain scenarios resolve to a single truth without manual intervention.

title: Zero-trust access boundaries around a container entrypoint that ignores signals
spec: Map the principle of least privilege onto a container entrypoint that ignores signals to prevent lateral movement if a neighboring service is compromised. Graceful shutdown never happens and in-flight requests are killed. Success: names one privilege separation boundary and the validation performed at runtime.
result: Boundary: run the entrypoint as a distinct non-root user with a dedicated seccomp profile that denies signal-sending syscalls (kill, tgkill, tkkill) toward processes outside its own PID namespace, enforced at the container runtime level rather than inside the process. Rationale: an entrypoint that ignores or fails to handle SIGTERM cannot be trusted to release resources on shutdown, so least privilege says it should not hold capabilities that matter during shutdown or that a compromised neighbor could exploit. Placing it in its own PID namespace plus a no-new-privileges flag means a compromised neighboring service cannot signal it, ptrace it, or pivot into its privileges; the boundary is the kernel-enforced isolation between containers, not the entrypoint's own signal handling. Runtime validation: at startup, the entrypoint (or a wrapper) verifies its effective UID is the expected non-root user, confirms no ambient capabilities remain (checking /proc/self/status CapEff is empty or minimal), and confirms seccomp is in filter mode by reading /proc/self/status Seccomp. If any check fails, it exits rather than serving traffic. This is a checkable claim about a standard mechanism; I have not verified a specific deployment or codebase, so no version numbers or product names are asserted.
